newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia and states agree A$5 bln tax pact -paper.
newsitem.headline: Australia and states agree A$5 bln tax pact -paper.

text.p: The Australian government agreed late on Tuesday night with Australia's states on a A$5 billion package of new federal taxes to replace those state taxes struck down by the High Court, The Australian Financial Review newspaper said on Wednesday.
"The new uniform national taxes are understood to be a 8.1 cent per litre tax on petrol, a 15 percent alcohol tax and a A$167 a kilo tax on tobacco," the Financial Review said.

"Under the system, the federal goverment would then reimburse the state government for the revenue their taxes would have raised, with any excess going back to the wholesalers to minimise the price impact on consumers," the newspaper said.

The High Court, in a landmark four to three majority decision released on Tuesday, struck down state tobacco, alcohol and petrol franchise fees. The court ruled the fees were in fact excise duties, which only the national government can raise under Australia's constitution.
Treasurer Peter Costello told reporters on Tuesday the federal government would help the states raise the lost revenues, but did not provide further details.
The newspaper said the total federal tax take under the new system would be around A$6.5 billion, compared with the A$5 billion raised by the now-invalid state taxes.
"But more than A$1 billion will be immediately redistributed to the states to be passed back to the wholesalers," the newspaper said.
The governments were concerned to avoid any increase in petrol prices, but officials setting up the complicated scheme believe cigarette prices could rise in some states.

"Complications will also arise because the 15 percent alcohol tax will be applied irrespective of alcohol content, although many states impose lower taxes on low alcohol beers," the Financial Review said.
The petrol tax would apply to all fuels, including diesel, the newspaper said.

Separately, Queensland Treasurer Joan Sheldon said in a statement that Queensland had joined with the other states and territories to officially ask the federal government to set up proposed safety net arrangements for taxes levied on petroleum, alcohol and tobacco.
"This request followed extensive discussions between the States and the Commonwealth to formulate the safety net plan," Sheldon said.
"It was a precondition of both Queensland and the Commonwealth that prices to the states' consumers would not be increased under such arrangements," she said.

After discussions between Queensland's Treasury officials and the fuel companies, the companies had given in-principle agreement not to increse petrol prices if they were reimbursed by the State, Sheldon said.
